description: One cup of all-purpose flour weighs 120 grams, spooned and levelled. Convert any amount between cups and grams, with the table and a worked example.

steps: Multiply by the weight of one cup: 2.5 × 120 g.
examples.title: 2 1/2 cups of flour to grams

steps: Divide by the weight of one cup: 180 ÷ 120.
examples.title: 180 g of flour to cups

faqs.answer: 120 grams, when the cup is spooned and levelled. That is the figure on King Arthur Baking's ingredient weight chart, and it is the standard most US recipes are written around.
faqs.question: How many grams are in a cup of all-purpose flour?

faqs.answer: Because a cup of flour weighs whatever the measuring method makes it weigh. A scooped cup packs in more flour, up to 140 grams or so. A spooned-and-levelled cup holds 120 grams. The charts disagree because the methods disagree, not because the flour changed.
faqs.question: Why do some charts say 125 g or 140 g?

faqs.answer: Just over 4 cups. 500 ÷ 120 = 4.17 cups, which is 4 cups plus about 2 1/2 tablespoons.
faqs.question: How many cups is 500 g of all-purpose flour?

faqs.answer: Only if the recipe tells you to. Sifting makes flour lighter, so a sifted cup weighs less than 120 grams. '1 cup flour, sifted' means measure first, then sift. '1 cup sifted flour' means sift first, and the weight will be lower.
faqs.question: Should I sift flour before measuring?

faqs.answer: Yes. King Arthur lists bread flour at 120 grams per cup as well. The flours differ in protein, not in how much a cup weighs.
faqs.question: Does bread flour weigh the same as all-purpose flour?

felicityNote: I keep the scale next to the flour canister now. It took one dry batch of muffins to convince me. The cup lied, the scale did not.

howToSteps.name: Fluff the flour
howToSteps.text: Stir the flour in its bag or canister with a spoon a few times. Flour settles and packs down in storage, and fluffing it up is what makes the cup weigh 120 grams instead of 140.

howToSteps.name: Spoon it into the cup
howToSteps.text: Spoon the flour into the measuring cup until it heaps over the top. Do not scoop with the cup itself. Scooping packs the flour down.

howToSteps.name: Level it off
howToSteps.text: Sweep the flat edge of a knife across the rim of the cup, back into the bag. The cup is now level and holds one cup.

howToSteps.name: Convert or weigh
howToSteps.text: Weigh the flour if you have a scale: one level cup should read 120 grams. Or use the converter above. Cups times 120 is grams, grams divided by 120 is cups.

name: All-Purpose Flour
sourceNote: King Arthur Baking lists all-purpose flour at 120 g per cup (4 1/4 oz).
title: Cups to Grams: All-Purpose Flour
tutorial: A cup of flour is not a fixed amount. Scoop the cup straight out of the bag and you can pack in 140 grams or more. Spoon it in lightly and level it off and the same cup holds 120 grams. That 20-gram swing is the difference between a tender crumb and a dry one, and it is why bakers weigh flour instead of scooping it.

The number on this page comes from King Arthur Baking's ingredient weight chart: one cup of all-purpose flour, spooned and levelled, weighs 120 grams. Spooned and levelled means you fluff the flour up with a spoon, spoon it into the measuring cup until it heaps over the top, then sweep a knife across the rim. No tapping, no shaking the cup down.

Use the converter in either direction. A recipe in cups becomes grams when you want the accuracy of the scale. A recipe in grams becomes cups when the scale is in a drawer somewhere and you are already halfway through mixing. Both directions use the same number: 120 grams per cup.

If you only remember one thing, remember the halves. Half a cup is 60 grams, a quarter cup is 30 grams, two cups is 240 grams. Most recipes land on those numbers, and once they are in your head you barely need the converter at all.

One more thing worth knowing: this is for unsifted flour, straight from the bag. Sifting fluffs flour up and a sifted cup weighs less. If a recipe says '1 cup flour, sifted', measure first and sift after. If it says '1 cup sifted flour', sift first, and know the cup will weigh less than 120 grams.
